question: Which deed offers the grantee the greatest protection because the grantor warrants against title defects arising both during and before the grantor's period of ownership?
choice_a: Special warranty deed
choice_b: Quitclaim deed
choice_c: General warranty deed
choice_d: Bargain and sale deed
explanation: A general warranty deed contains the full set of common-law title covenants (seisin, right to convey, against encumbrances, quiet enjoyment, warranty, and further assurance) and the grantor warrants title against defects arising at any time, even before the grantor owned the property. This makes it the strongest deed for a buyer and is the standard deed used in most arm's-length residential sales.
source_note: Common-law deed covenants tested on the national/general portion of the PSI Mississippi real estate broker exam (MREC Candidate Information Bulletin, 10/1/2023); standard property-law doctrine covering full covenants of general warranty deeds.

question: A deed in which the grantor warrants title only against defects that arose during the grantor's own period of ownership, and not against defects that arose before the grantor acquired title, is best described as a:
choice_a: General warranty deed
choice_b: Quitclaim deed
choice_c: Deed of trust
choice_d: Special warranty deed
explanation: A special (limited) warranty deed limits the grantor's warranty to the time the grantor personally held title. It is commonly used by fiduciaries, corporate sellers, banks disposing of REO property, and executors/trustees who cannot personally vouch for events before their ownership.
source_note: Standard property-law distinction between general and special warranty deeds; national real estate license exam content, PSI/MREC candidate bulletin general portion.

question: A quitclaim deed is most commonly used to:
choice_a: Convey whatever interest, if any, the grantor currently holds, without any warranties of title
choice_b: Guarantee that the grantor holds clear, marketable title
choice_c: Transfer title automatically upon the grantor's death without probate
choice_d: Create a lien against real property to secure a debt
explanation: A quitclaim deed conveys only whatever interest the grantor actually has at the time of conveyance, with no covenants or warranties whatsoever. If the grantor has no interest, the grantee receives nothing. It is the weakest form of deed for a purchaser but is widely used to clear title clouds, transfer property between family members, or release a claimed interest.
source_note: Fundamental deed classification tested nationally on real estate licensing exams, including the PSI Mississippi broker exam general/national portion.

question: A title company discovers a potential cloud on title caused by a former spouse's unreleased dower/curtesy or homestead interest. This cloud is most commonly cleared by obtaining which type of deed from that individual?
choice_a: General warranty deed
choice_b: Quitclaim deed
choice_c: Bargain and sale deed
choice_d: Special warranty deed
explanation: Because a quitclaim deed conveys any interest the signer might have without asserting or admitting that any interest actually exists, it is the standard tool for clearing clouds on title, such as a former spouse's unreleased marital or homestead interest, an heir's unclear claim, or a boundary/name discrepancy.
source_note: Standard title-clearing practice in real estate closings, part of the national deed-and-title-transfer content outline for PSI real estate exams.

question: A bargain and sale deed implies that the grantor:
choice_a: Warrants against all title defects, including those that arose before the grantor's ownership
choice_b: Has no interest whatsoever in the property being conveyed
choice_c: Holds and possesses title to the property but makes no warranties against encumbrances or prior defects
choice_d: Is conveying title only upon the grantor's death
explanation: A bargain and sale deed implies, by its language, that the grantor holds title and possesses the property, but it contains no express warranties against encumbrances or title defects (unless a covenant against the grantor's own acts is added). It sits between a warranty deed and a quitclaim deed in the level of protection it affords the grantee.
source_note: Traditional deed-classification content on the national portion of real estate licensing exams; bargain and sale deeds remain in common use in several U.S. jurisdictions.

question: For legal title to actually pass from grantor to grantee, a validly executed deed must be:
choice_a: Recorded in the county land records
choice_b: Witnessed by two disinterested parties in every state
choice_c: Notarized before a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: Delivered by the grantor and accepted by the grantee during the grantor's lifetime
explanation: Delivery of the deed by the grantor with the intent to convey title, and acceptance by the grantee, is the act that actually transfers title. Recording is not required to pass title between the parties; it only gives constructive notice to third parties and protects the grantee's priority against later claimants.
source_note: Core common-law requirement of delivery and acceptance for valid conveyance, standard content on the national portion of the PSI real estate broker exam.

question: Which of the following is an essential element required for a deed to be legally valid?
choice_a: A legal description of the property sufficient to identify it with reasonable certainty
choice_b: A statement of the exact sale price actually paid by the grantee
choice_c: The buyer's mortgage loan account number
choice_d: An attached title insurance policy
explanation: A valid deed must include, among other elements, a competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, words of conveyance (granting clause), a legally sufficient description of the property, consideration (which need not state the actual price), and the grantor's signature. The exact sale price, a loan number, and a title policy are not required elements of the deed itself.
source_note: Statute of Frauds and common-law elements of a valid deed, general/national content tested on state real estate licensing exams.

question: The clause in a deed, typically beginning with the words 'to have and to hold,' that defines the type and quantity of the estate being conveyed to the grantee is the:
choice_a: Granting clause
choice_b: Habendum clause
choice_c: Acknowledgment
choice_d: Reddendum clause
explanation: The habendum clause ('to have and to hold') follows the granting clause and defines the estate being conveyed (for example, a fee simple absolute or a life estate) and any limitations on that estate. The granting clause, by contrast, contains the actual words of conveyance identifying the parties and stating the grantor's intent to transfer the property.
source_note: Standard deed-anatomy terminology in national real estate license exam content.

question: Which of the following is an example of involuntary alienation of title to real property?
choice_a: A homeowner selling a house using a general warranty deed
choice_b: A homeowner gifting real estate to a relative using a quitclaim deed
choice_c: Property acquired by a government entity through eminent domain
choice_d: Property transferred to a named beneficiary under the owner's properly executed will
explanation: Involuntary alienation transfers title without the owner's consent, such as through eminent domain/condemnation, foreclosure, tax sale, adverse possession, or escheat. Voluntary alienation, by contrast, includes sales, gifts, and transfers made under a will (devise), all of which reflect the owner's own decision to convey the property.
source_note: Standard classification of voluntary vs. involuntary alienation, national/general property law content on real estate licensing exams.

question: When a property owner dies leaving a valid will that names a beneficiary to receive real estate, that transfer of title is known as:
choice_a: Intestate succession
choice_b: Escheat
choice_c: Adverse possession
choice_d: Devise (testate succession)
explanation: A gift of real property made by will is called a devise, and the recipient is a devisee; this process is testate succession because the decedent left a valid will directing how the property should pass. It is generally treated as voluntary alienation because it reflects the decedent's own expressed intent.
source_note: Standard probate/title-transfer terminology, national portion of real estate licensing exam content.

question: If a property owner dies without a valid will, real property passes to the decedent's heirs according to state intestacy statutes through a process known as:
choice_a: Descent (intestate succession)
choice_b: Devise
choice_c: Escheat
choice_d: Condemnation
explanation: When a person dies intestate (without a valid will), title passes by descent, meaning state intestacy statutes determine which heirs receive the property and in what shares, typically through an administrator appointed by the probate court rather than an executor named in a will.
source_note: Standard intestate succession/descent terminology, national/general content on real estate licensing exams; based on universally applied intestacy principles reflected in state probate codes.

question: If a property owner dies intestate and no heirs can be located or ascertained, title to the real property will ultimately:
choice_a: Transfer to the deceased's largest unsecured creditor
choice_b: Escheat to the state
choice_c: Become subject to adverse possession by any claimant who occupies it
choice_d: Remain in perpetual probate administration indefinitely
explanation: Escheat is the process by which title to property reverts to the state when an owner dies intestate with no ascertainable heirs. It ensures that real property never remains permanently without a legal owner and is a form of involuntary alienation.
source_note: Escheat doctrine, standard national real estate exam content covering involuntary methods of title transfer.

question: To acquire title to real property through adverse possession, a claimant's possession of the land must generally be:
choice_a: Secret, sporadic, and with the record owner's express permission
choice_b: Recorded with the county recorder within one year of entry
choice_c: Open, notorious, continuous, hostile, and exclusive for the statutory period
choice_d: Approved in writing in advance by the record title holder
explanation: Adverse possession requires possession that is open and notorious (visible and obvious), continuous for the statutory period set by state law, hostile (without the owner's permission and under a claim of right), and exclusive (not shared with the true owner or the public). Permissive or secret possession does not satisfy the doctrine, and the claimant must typically also bring a quiet title action to perfect record title.
source_note: Common-law adverse possession elements, standard content on the involuntary-transfer portion of national real estate licensing exams.

question: The government's power to take private property for public use, provided the owner receives just compensation, is called:
choice_a: Escheat
choice_b: Police power
choice_c: Adverse possession
choice_d: Eminent domain
explanation: Eminent domain is the sovereign power of government (or an authorized public utility) to condemn and take private property for a public use, such as a highway or utility easement, upon payment of just compensation to the owner, as required by the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause. Condemnation is the legal proceeding used to exercise that power.
source_note: U.S. Constitution, Fifth Amendment Takings Clause; standard eminent domain content on the national portion of real estate licensing exams.

question: When a lender forecloses on a defaulted mortgage and the property is sold at a foreclosure sale to satisfy the debt, this transfer of title is classified as:
choice_a: Involuntary alienation
choice_b: Voluntary alienation
choice_c: Testate succession
choice_d: A bargain and sale conveyance made by the original owner
explanation: Foreclosure transfers title without the defaulting owner's consent, making it a form of involuntary alienation, alongside eminent domain, tax sale, adverse possession, and escheat. Title typically passes via a sheriff's deed, trustee's deed, or similar instrument depending on whether the foreclosure is judicial or non-judicial (power-of-sale).
source_note: Standard foreclosure and involuntary-alienation classification, national portion of real estate licensing exam content.

question: The primary legal purpose of recording a deed in the county land records is to:
choice_a: Transfer legal title from the grantor to the grantee
choice_b: Provide constructive notice to the world of the grantee's ownership interest
choice_c: Guarantee the accuracy of the property's legal description
choice_d: Satisfy the requirements of the Statute of Frauds
explanation: Recording does not itself transfer title (delivery and acceptance do that); rather, it places the conveyance in the public record so that all subsequent parties are charged with constructive notice of the grantee's interest, which protects the grantee's priority against later purchasers, lienholders, or claimants under the state's recording act.
source_note: Recording act theory and constructive notice, foundational national/general content on real estate licensing exams.

question: A prospective buyer inspects a property before closing and sees someone other than the seller in actual physical possession of it. This observation places the buyer under a legal duty to investigate that person's rights, a concept known as:
choice_a: Constructive notice
choice_b: Actual notice
choice_c: Inquiry notice
choice_d: Record notice
explanation: Visible possession by someone other than the record owner puts a buyer on inquiry notice, obligating the buyer to reasonably investigate the possessor's claim (such as an unrecorded lease or contract for deed). This differs from constructive notice, which arises from properly recorded documents, and actual notice, which is direct personal knowledge of a fact.
source_note: Doctrine of inquiry notice arising from open possession, standard title-and-notice content on national real estate licensing exams.

question: The complete recorded history of transfers, liens, and encumbrances affecting a specific parcel of real property is called the:
choice_a: Abstract of judgment
choice_b: Plat map
choice_c: Certificate of occupancy
choice_d: Chain of title
explanation: The chain of title is the chronological sequence of recorded documents showing every transfer of ownership and every recorded encumbrance affecting a parcel, traced back to its original source. A title examiner reviews the chain of title to identify defects, gaps, or clouds before a title insurance policy is issued.
source_note: Title examination terminology, standard national content on real estate licensing exams covering title recording and title insurance.

question: An owner's title insurance policy protects:
choice_a: The buyer/owner, and typically their heirs, against covered title defects for as long as they or their heirs retain an interest in the property
choice_b: The lender for the full life of the mortgage loan, regardless of the loan balance
choice_c: The seller against any future decline in the property's market value
choice_d: The real estate broker against commission disputes arising from the sale
explanation: An owner's title insurance policy is a one-time-premium policy purchased at closing that protects the buyer (and generally their heirs or devisees) against covered title defects, liens, or claims that existed but were undiscovered as of the policy date, for as long as the insured retains an interest in the property.
source_note: Standard title insurance mechanics, national/general portion of real estate licensing exam content.

question: A lender's (mortgagee's) title insurance policy:
choice_a: Directly protects the buyer's equity in the home against title defects
choice_b: Is typically issued in an amount equal to the loan amount and decreases in coverage as the loan balance is paid down
choice_c: Remains at a fixed coverage amount regardless of the outstanding loan balance
choice_d: Automatically transfers its coverage to a subsequent buyer of the property
explanation: A lender's title policy protects only the lender's security interest, in an amount equal to the loan amount, and its coverage generally decreases as the principal balance is paid down, ultimately terminating once the loan is satisfied. It provides no protection to the buyer/owner, who must purchase a separate owner's policy for that protection.
source_note: Standard distinction between owner's and lender's title insurance policies, national real estate exam content.

question: In a real estate escrow closing, the escrow agent's basic legal duty is to:
choice_a: Represent the buyer's interests exclusively throughout the transaction
choice_b: Independently determine the fair market value of the property being sold
choice_c: Act as a neutral third party who holds documents and funds and disburses them only once all conditions of the escrow instructions have been satisfied
choice_d: Negotiate the final sale price on behalf of either the buyer or the seller
explanation: An escrow agent is a neutral, dual agent for both buyer and seller who holds funds, the deed, and other closing documents in trust, and disburses or records them only after every condition specified in the mutually agreed escrow instructions has been satisfied. The escrow agent does not represent either party's interests or negotiate terms.
source_note: Standard escrow/closing agent duties, national portion of real estate licensing exam content.

question: At closing, recurring expenses such as property taxes, HOA dues, or insurance premiums are typically prorated between the buyer and seller in order to:
choice_a: Eliminate the need for a title search before closing
choice_b: Satisfy the requirements of the Statute of Frauds
choice_c: Avoid the need to record the deed after closing
choice_d: Allocate each expense fairly based on the portion of the billing period each party actually owned the property
explanation: Proration divides recurring, periodic expenses (and sometimes prepaid items or rents) between buyer and seller based on the number of days each party owned the property during the applicable billing or tax period, ensuring neither party pays for costs attributable to the other's period of ownership.
source_note: Standard closing/settlement statement mechanics, national portion of real estate licensing exam content.

question: Two individuals hold title to a property as joint tenants with right of survivorship. When one joint tenant dies, that deceased joint tenant's interest:
choice_a: Passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s), outside of probate
choice_b: Passes according to the terms of the deceased joint tenant's will
choice_c: Becomes subject to intestate succession under state law
choice_d: Escheats to the state
explanation: The defining feature of joint tenancy is the right of survivorship: upon a joint tenant's death, that owner's interest automatically vests in the surviving joint tenant(s) by operation of law, bypassing probate entirely and overriding any contrary provision in the deceased's will. This differs from tenancy in common, where a deceased owner's interest passes to their heirs or devisees through probate.
source_note: Common-law right of survivorship in joint tenancy, standard national content on methods of holding and passing title at death for real estate licensing exams.
